native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black respondents (NLSY-79 processed file), incarceration (ever_jailed = 1, jailed 1985–1994) is associated with substantially lower wealth by 1996 at every economic-status level, where 'income levels' are proxied — as a stated assumption, since no income variable exists — by rank-based quartiles of baseline composite_wealth_1985. Within every baseline-wealth quartile, jailed black respondents gained far less wealth from 1985 to 1996 than non-jailed peers (mean jailed-minus-non-jailed gaps: −$19,003 in Q1, −$16,061 in Q2, −$41,742 in Q3, −$58,317 in Q4; pooled −$33,489), while at baseline the groups were nearly equal (gaps of roughly $0 to −$16,000). In absolute dollars the wealth penalty of incarceration is largest for high-baseline black respondents — the top-quartile jailed group's mean wealth actually fell (Δ = −$5,043) while non-jailed top-quartile peers gained +$53,274 (median DiD −$14,876) — whereas for low-baseline respondents the penalty manifests as floor-level stagnation: medians of composite_wealth_1996 are $0 for both groups (median DiD ≈ 0 due to ties at zero), yet jailed means remain only ~21–35% of non-jailed means and 57% of jailed respondents sit at exactly zero wealth in 1996 versus 33% of non-jailed. The jailed/non-jailed mean-wealth ratio falls from 0.34–0.86 in 1985 to 0.19–0.35 by 1996 in every quartile. Male-only results (n=143 jailed vs 1,322 non-jailed) show the same pattern with larger gaps (Q4 mean DiD −$76,192); the black jailed female cell (n=16, all wealth medians $0) is reported but too small for separate inference. A jail wealth penalty also appears for white respondents (mean Δ96 DiD −$92,678), so the direction is not black-specific; it is especially consequential for black respondents because jail incidence is far higher (159/3,013 ≈ 5.3%, vs 69/7,099 ≈ 1.0% for white). This is an observational association, not a causal effect: mechanical wealth suppression during 1985–1994 incarceration, baseline imbalance ($320 vs $764 median composite_wealth_1985), small jailed cells, absence of income/age/incarceration-timing fields, duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent, and ever_jailed being the only incarceration indicator (no residence field exists) all preclude a causal reading.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Profiled data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; documented 6 columns; no missing values; 1,899 duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent; confirmed no income, age, or residence fields). 2) Restricted to race=='black' (n=3,013); built economic-status strata as rank-based quartiles of composite_wealth_1985 (deterministic random tie-breaking, seed 0); cell sizes by ever_jailed: 47/36/42/34 jailed vs 707/717/711/719 non-jailed. 3) Computed levels (median and mean of composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996) and changes d90 = 1990−1985, d96 = 1996−1985 by stratum × ever_jailed. 4) Built the DiD table (jailed Δ minus non-jailed Δ) for medians and means, pooled and male-only (female jailed n=16 flagged). 5) Triple-difference robustness using white (primary) and all-non-black (secondary) reference groups. 6) Verified floor effects (zero-wealth shares, jailed/non-jailed mean ratios). Executed script: analysis/nls_incarceration_analysis.py; console output preserved in analysis/output.txt.

sub_hypo.relations: Zero-wealth floor effects mask differences in medians, while lower means and a greater zero-wealth share indicate poorer wealth outcomes among jailed respondents.
